title: Environment and Sustainable Development
summary: ## The environment

The environment is all the living and non-living things occurring naturally on Earth. It is made up of biotic (living) components — plants, animals, birds, forests — and abiotic (non-living) components — air, water, rocks, the sun. These influence each other.
As more goods are produced, more resources are used up. Factory smoke and sewage pollute air and water, and the destruction of nature harms human, social and economic life.
## Significance of the environment

(1) It provides both renewable and non-renewable resources. Renewable resources, such as forests and fish, are replenished over time. Non-renewable resources, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals, run out; all current energy sources may be used up within 50–75 years.
(2) It absorbs harmful wastes — smoke, sewage and industrial effluents — and cleans and recycles them through natural processes.
(3) It sustains life through biodiversity, the variety of life forms and their links with the non-living environment.
(4) It has aesthetic value: scenery and landscapes.
## Pollution

Pollution is an undesirable change in the quality of a natural resource or ecosystem that harms living beings. A pollutant is the waste or substance that causes it, such as smoke, dust, poisonous gases, effluents or sewage.

Air pollution comes from harmful chemicals and particles in the air, such as sulphur and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and metals. Man-made sources: smoke from power plants and factories, vehicle exhaust, farm chemicals and dust, paint and aerosol fumes, and methane from landfills. Natural sources: dust from barren land, methane from cattle, smoke from wildfires, and volcanoes. Effects: breathing difficulty, coughing and wheezing, heart and lung disease, and early death (WHO: 2.4 million deaths a year).

Water pollution is the contamination of lakes, rivers, seas and groundwater. Sources: sewage and sewage-treatment discharge, industrial effluents, farm runoff of pesticides and fertilisers, dirty storm water, heated or radioactive water from power plants, oil spills, and algae. Effects: diseases such as cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea; changes in the water's chemistry (acidity, temperature); and the death of fish and birds, which disturbs the natural food cycle.

Noise pollution is excessive, displeasing noise. Sources: traffic, industry (stone crushing, sawing), construction, and household appliances. Effects: harm to physical and mental health — stress, aggression, hypertension, sleeplessness and hearing loss.
## Degradation

Soil degradation is an undesirable change in soil quality: the soil loses nutrients and humus and becomes unfit for crops. Causes: (1) excessive chemical fertilisers and pesticides, which make the soil acidic, saline and toxic; (2) waterlogging from over-irrigation; (3) overgrazing, which removes plant cover and causes erosion. Effects: lower yields, polluted groundwater, loss of green cover and biodiversity, and desertification.

Habitat degradation is the loss of a habitat's ability to support native life because of human activity. It reduces the carrying capacity of the area, upsets food chains and causes extinctions. Causes: deforestation and timber extraction, turning forest into farmland, urban expansion, soil erosion and desertification, and slash-and-burn farming. Effects: floods, droughts, crop failure, disease, loss of ecosystem services and climate change.
## Depletion of resources

Resource depletion is the exhaustion of raw materials in an area, through farming, fishing and mining. Petroleum, natural gas, coal, uranium and gold are becoming scarce because of over-exploitation and population growth. Agencies that protect the environment include UNEP, EPA, IPCC and India's Ministry of Environment and Forests, as well as NGOs.
## Sustainable development

The Brundtland Report defines sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." It is a long-term concept. All its definitions require that we see the world as a whole: smoke from North America affects Asia, and pesticides in Bangladesh harm fish off West Bengal.
We can contribute in three ways:
(1) Resources: find substitutes for non-renewable resources — solar, wind, hydro, tidal power and gobar gas — and use renewable resources judiciously.
(2) Recycling: recycle paper to save trees; reuse rainwater through rainwater harvesting.
(3) Reducing: restrain consumption to basic needs — walk, use the stairs, switch off lights and fans.

'The environment sustains life through biodiversity.' Explain.
The environment supports a variety of life forms, which adapt, evolve and depend on each other and on air, water and soil. Preserving the environment preserves this biodiversity and life itself.

or: 'Pollution harms the health of living beings.' Explain.

Polluted air causes breathing and heart problems; polluted water causes cholera and typhoid and kills fish; noise causes stress and hearing loss. So pollution harms the health of humans, animals and plants.

vsa: How does recycling help sustainable development?
Recycling means using things again. Recycling paper saves trees, since paper is made from wood pulp, and rainwater harvesting saves scarce water, so resources last for future generations.
October 2024

or: What is meant by judicious use of resources?
Using resources carefully and only as needed — avoiding waste, using renewable resources at a rate they can renew, and replacing non-renewables with solar, wind and biogas.

vsa: How does the environment absorb harmful wastes?
Smoke from chimneys and vehicles, sewage and industrial effluents are absorbed by air, water and soil, and are cleaned and recycled by natural processes — as long as they are within its capacity.

Suggest two steps a farmer can take to reduce soil degradation.

(1) Use chemical fertilisers and pesticides sparingly and use organic manure.
(2) Avoid over-irrigation (and drain fields) and prevent overgrazing by keeping plant cover.

sa: Explain the sources of air pollution.

Man-made: smoke from power plants and factories, exhaust from vehicles, farm chemicals and dust, fumes of paint and aerosol sprays, and methane from landfills.
Natural: dust from barren land, methane from cattle digestion, smoke from wildfires, and gases and ash from volcanoes.
What are the causes of habitat degradation?

(1) Deforestation and wood extraction for timber.
(2) Conversion of forest land into farmland.
(3) Urban expansion into natural habitats.
(4) Soil erosion and desertification.
(5) Slash-and-burn agriculture.
'Habitat degradation reduces the carrying capacity of an area.' Explain.

Carrying capacity is the number of plants and animals of a species an area can support.
When forests are cut and land is cleared, food and shelter are lost, so fewer animals and plants can survive there.
Populations fall, food chains are upset, and species may become extinct.
Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources with examples.

Renewable resources are replenished naturally over time and can be used without running out if used carefully — forests, fish, water, solar and wind energy.
Non-renewable resources are exhausted as they are used and cannot be replaced — coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals. They must be used carefully for future generations.
What is noise pollution? What are its effects?

Noise pollution is excessive, displeasing noise from traffic, industry, construction and appliances.
Effects: annoyance and aggression, stress, hypertension, sleep disturbance, heart problems and noise-induced hearing loss.
What is meant by soil degradation? State its causes.

Soil degradation is an undesirable change in soil quality: it loses nutrients and humus and becomes unfit for crops.
Causes: excessive chemical fertilisers and pesticides; waterlogging from over-irrigation; overgrazing, which leads to erosion.
la: How can we contribute to sustainable development?

Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, and we must see the world as a whole.
(1) Resources: find substitutes for non-renewable resources — solar cookers and lanterns, windmills, hydro, tidal power and gobar gas — and use renewable resources judiciously.
(2) Recycle: recycle paper to save trees, and harvest rainwater.
(3) Reduce: restrain consumption to basic needs — walk instead of driving, use the stairs, switch off unneeded fans and lights.
Governments and international bodies must also coordinate policy, since pollution crosses borders.
What is air pollution? State four natural sources and two effects.

Air pollution is the introduction into the atmosphere of chemicals, particles or biological matter that harm living beings or the environment, e.g. sulphur and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and particulates.
Natural sources: (1) dust from barren land; (2) methane from cattle; (3) smoke and carbon monoxide from wildfires; (4) sulphur, chlorine and ash from volcanoes.
Effects: (1) breathing difficulty, coughing and aggravated heart and lung disease; (2) more hospital admissions and premature deaths (2.4 million a year, WHO). Carbon dioxide also adds to global warming.
What is habitat degradation? Mention two causes and one effect.

Habitat degradation is the process by which a habitat loses its ability to support native life because of human activities, which reduces its carrying capacity.
Causes: (1) deforestation and timber extraction; (2) conversion of forests to farmland and urban expansion (also slash-and-burn farming and desertification).
Effect: loss of biodiversity and extinction of species, which upsets food chains. It also makes the area more prone to floods, droughts and crop failure.
Explain three major causes of soil degradation.

(1) Excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides makes the soil acidic, saline or alkaline, reduces humus, and adds toxins and heavy metals such as cadmium and lead.
(2) Waterlogging: over-irrigation without drainage raises the salt content, making soil unfit for crops and breeding mosquitoes.
(3) Overgrazing by animals removes plant cover and leaves the soil open to erosion.
Result: lower yields, polluted groundwater, loss of biodiversity and desertification.
Explain the significance of the environment.

(1) It provides renewable resources (forests, fish) and non-renewable resources (coal, petroleum).
(2) It absorbs and recycles wastes such as smoke, sewage and effluents.
(3) It sustains life through biodiversity.
(4) It has aesthetic value — scenery and landscapes that are part of human culture.
